programme: RELA and FOSL1 form the paired NF-κB/AP-1 inflammatory module: RELA (canonical NF-κB) and FOSL1 (Fra-1, AP-1 family) converge on composite κB/AP-1 promoter elements to drive the same set of endothelial/immune activation genes (IL6, TNF, CXCL8, ICAM1, VCAM1, SELE, MMP9, CCL2, BIRC3).
role_in_a: In bipolar disorder, RELA and FOSL1 are reported among the differentially expressed/dysregulated genes in peripheral and prefrontal transcriptomic profiling, consistent with the low-grade systemic inflammation repeatedly described in the disorder.
role_in_b: In stroke, RELA/NF-κB and FOSL1/AP-1 drive the post-ischemic endothelial activation and leukocyte-recruitment programme (adhesion molecule and cytokine induction) that accompanies vascular injury and blood-brain barrier compromise.
shared_axis: Neither disease is defined by this axis, but each independently recruits the same NF-κB/AP-1 inflammatory core in its own compartment — chronic low-grade inflammation in bipolar disorder and acute ischemic inflammation in stroke could be parallel activations of the same RELA-FOSL1 transcriptional module rather than a documented cross-disease mechanism.
reasoning: RELA and FOSL1 are the only two of the twelve factors with literature placing them in both diseases separately, and their target overlap (IL6, CCL2, VCAM1, ICAM1, MMP9) is a recognizable, real inflammatory module rather than a coincidence of the target lists. The connection between the two diseases through this module is not itself documented anywhere in the retrieved record, so it rests on the general premise that inflammation is a shared feature of both conditions, which caps the strength at moderate. The other ten factors (TCF20, LRRFIP1, SOX17, BRCA1, FOXJ1, SOX4, GLI1, RXRA, ZNF521, ATF6) span developmental, ciliogenesis, ER-stress and DNA-repair biology with no target or functional overlap with RELA/FOSL1 or each other, so they were not folded into the account.
support: PMID 39828023 (RELA among genes in a regulatory-network/therapeutic-prediction study framed around bipolar disorder); PMID 42621097 (RELA/NF-κB signalling drives stroke progression); PMID 42196418 (RELA/NF-κB-linked inflammatory genes enriched among ischemic stroke and cardiovascular disease genes); PMID 40539026 (FOSL1 implicated via IL-17 pathway transcriptomics in bipolar disorder); PMID 40727846 (FOSL1 among transcriptomic signatures spanning bipolar disorder and related psychiatric conditions); PMID 37775708 (FOSL1 implicated in shared endothelial metabolic shifts in stroke).
how_to_falsify: Perform ChIP-seq/CUT&RUN for RELA and FOSL1 in a disease-relevant cell type from each side (e.g., PBMCs or iPSC-neurons from bipolar disorder patients; cerebral endothelial cells after ischemic insult) and test whether the two factors co-occupy the same composite κB/AP-1 elements at IL6, VCAM1, CCL2 and MMP9, and whether knocking down FOSL1 blunts RELA-driven induction of these genes (or vice versa) in both settings. If co-occupancy or functional dependence is absent in either tissue, the proposed shared module does not hold.
caveats: The tissue pairing is blood (bipolar disorder) versus brain (stroke), so any shared axis is necessarily a parallel, same-pathway activation in different compartments, not a demonstrated direct interaction between the two diseases. The concordance calls rest on only 15 patient-group comparisons drawn from 4 independent cohort pairs, and even the best-supported factors here reach only 12/15 (80%) concordance, not the near-total agreement seen in stronger pairs. Classic inflammatory/tissue master regulators (CEBPB, CEBPD, RUNX3, JUNB) were excluded as tissue-generic and should not be read back into this account, and none of the six single-view factors (FOS, RERE, HIVEP2, NFATC1, MIXL1, OVOL1) — despite FOS being an obvious AP-1 partner one might otherwise reach for — were used, since they only topped one patient subgroup.
